synopsis: A continuous first-person flight through the dense debris field of the main asteroid belt between Mars and Jupiter.

shots.prompt:
One continuous 15-second first-person flight at 24 fps, filmed as if the camera itself is the spacecraft, moving forward without pause for the entire take. Seconds 0-4 are calm and wide: the real body fills one side of the frame, lit hard from the side, the far sun flaring at the frame edge, and the camera is already drifting forward. Seconds 4-6 accelerate toward the obstacle field and the first objects slide into frame. Seconds 6-13 race through the field itself: objects rush past on both sides and overhead, the nearest ones blurring, fine particles streaking past the lens, objects colliding and bursting apart, the body still showing through the gaps. Seconds 13-15 plunge into the densest part and the frame fills with the climax, the brightest and most overwhelming moment of the whole take, still moving forward as it ends. One continuous take, no cut, no fade, no scene change, and the camera never stops or hovers. Nothing of the vehicle is visible: no cockpit, no hull, no instruments, no HUD. No text, no captions, no logos, no watermark, no people. Sound: diegetic only and locked to what is on screen, a deep low rumble running under the whole flight, quiet and distant at the start, sharp impacts hitting exactly when objects collide, the whole sound field growing continuously and reaching its loudest and fullest in the final two seconds. No music, no voice, no narration.

A first-person camera glides forward through the main asteroid belt between Mars and Jupiter. Seconds 0-4 present a vast space expanse illuminated by harsh side-lighting from the distant Sun, exposing dark grey silicate and metallic boulders floating against a pitch-black starry background. Seconds 4-6 show an increase in velocity as mountain-sized irregular rocks drift into frame, their pockmarked craters throwing sharp, deep shadows. Seconds 6-13 accelerate through a dense orbital debris stream, where house-sized asteroids tumble past on all sides, foreground rocks streak with intense motion blur, and smaller fragments violently collide, shattering into sparkling dust clouds while Jupiter shines dimly far behind. Seconds 13-15 plunge into a clustered wall of tumbling rocky debris, filling the entire vertical frame with blinding reflected highlights and high-energy gravel impacts before crashing directly into a massive asteroid face. Sound starts as a low, quiet hum, building with crisp metallic impacts during collisions, and swelling into a deafening roar in the final two seconds.

first_comment: Which asteroid would you like to explore up close? ☄️
caption:
A first-person flight passes through the main asteroid belt between Mars and Jupiter.

This region contains millions of silicate and metallic rocks, ranging from tiny dust grains to tumbling boulders hundreds of kilometers across.

NASA's Galileo spacecraft flew through this zone in 1991, capturing the first close-up images of asteroids Gaspra and Ida.

A high-speed journey through this belt remains impossible because relative orbital velocities reaching eighteen kilometers per second turn even microscopic gravel into catastrophic armor-piercing impacts.

This is a simulation, not real footage. Would you navigate through an asteroid belt if shield technology existed?
